tests.name: Quick Check
tests.description: Timed check on Food Safety Legislation & HACCP

questions.question: Q: What are the three main requirements of the Food Safety Act 1990?
questions.correctAnswer: Food must be safe to eat, not harmful to health, and labelled and described accurately (not misleadingly).

questions.question: Q: What is the role of an Environmental Health Officer?
questions.correctAnswer: EHOs enforce food safety law by inspecting food premises (often unannounced), taking food samples, issuing improvement notices, and closing businesses that pose an immediate health risk.

questions.question: Q: What does HACCP stand for?
questions.correctAnswer: Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Food Safety Legislation & HACCP

questions.question: Q: List the three types of food safety hazard with an example of each.
questions.correctAnswer: Biological (e.g. Salmonella bacteria), chemical (e.g. cleaning fluid contamination), physical (e.g. glass, bone, or packaging in food).

questions.question: Q: What is a Critical Control Point (CCP)?
questions.correctAnswer: A step in the food process where control is essential to prevent, eliminate, or reduce a food safety hazard to an acceptable level (e.g. cooking to 75°C, chilling below 5°C).

questions.question: Q: Name the 7 principles of HACCP.
questions.correctAnswer: 1. Conduct hazard analysis, 2. Identify CCPs, 3. Set critical limits, 4. Monitor CCPs, 5. Establish corrective actions, 6. Verify the system works, 7. Keep documentation and records.

questions.question: Q: What is the Food Hygiene Rating Scheme and what is the range of scores?
questions.correctAnswer: A scheme where EHOs rate food businesses from 0 (urgent improvement necessary) to 5 (very good) based on hygiene, structure, and management. Ratings are displayed publicly.

questions.question: Q: Explain the due diligence defence.
questions.correctAnswer: A business can defend itself against a food safety charge by proving it took all reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence to avoid the offence — for example, having HACCP records, staff training logs, and supplier checks.
